items.stem: A historian argues that the Columbian Exchange was an exchange of goods between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that spread prosperity to people on both sides of the Atlantic. Which response to this argument is most defensible?
options: (A) Introduced diseases alone caused the collapse of Native populations, so the only harm of the exchange was a biological accident that no one intended.
(B) Judged by modern standards of consent and free trade, the transfer of goods was voluntary exchange on both sides, which confirms the historian's claim of shared prosperity.
(C) Crops, animals, and diseases did move in both directions, but the exchange was asymmetric: Native peoples bore the epidemics and coerced labor, while Europeans gained most of the food and wealth.

(D) Potatoes transformed European diets and supported rapid population growth, which proves that the exchange raised living standards for ordinary people on both sides of the Atlantic over the long run.
items.explanation: The exchange really did move goods both ways -- wheat, horses, and cattle to the Americas; maize, potatoes, and tomatoes to the Old World. But 'spread prosperity to both sides' needs qualifying: the costs -- epidemics and forced labor -- fell overwhelmingly on Native peoples, while Europeans captured most of the material gains.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It makes disease the one and only cause of Native population collapse, leaving out Spanish violence, enslavement, and the uprooting of Native communities. It also treats a consequence of conquest as if it were disconnected from the conquest.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. It judges a 16th-century system built on conquest by modern free-market ideas, as if coercion and choice were the same thing. Prosperity that one side imposes is not the shared prosperity the historian claims.
option_explanations.C: Right. It accepts the real two-way movement of plants, animals, and diseases, then qualifies the prosperity claim with the asymmetry the evidence shows: Native peoples bore the demographic catastrophe and the forced labor, while Europeans gained the food and wealth.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It takes one crop's effect on Europe and stretches it to cover both hemispheres, ignoring the Native populations that were devastated rather than enriched.

items.fact_source: Two-way transfers: wheat, horses, cattle, pigs to the Americas; maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao to the Old World. Virgin-soil epidemics and coerced labor (encomienda grants, silver mining) devastated Native populations, while agricultural and mineral gains enriched Europe.

stimulus.text: In a 1542 written account addressed to the Spanish king, the Dominican friar Bartolome de las Casas -- who had earlier held an encomienda grant in Hispaniola -- described Native Americans as gentle and rational and condemned Spanish violence in the conquest. (Paraphrase; original in Spanish.)

items.stem: Which statement best evaluates the usefulness of this account as evidence of Native American societies before contact with Europeans?
options: (A) Because Las Casas judged the conquest by universal moral standards, his account gives a reliable, modern-style description of Native societies before Europeans arrived.

(B) Las Casas wrote to move the king to reform colonial policy, so the account is best evidence of the Spanish debate over Native treatment; for describing Native life itself, it must be checked against other sources.
(C) The account proves that Spanish violence was the single cause of the collapse of Native populations in the Caribbean, since Las Casas saw firsthand why so many Native people died.

(D) Las Casas described the Native people he knew in the Caribbean as peaceful and gentle, so his account can safely be generalized to show that Native societies across the entire Americas were nonviolent and untouched by conflict.
items.explanation: Las Casas was writing advocacy, not ethnography: he described Native people as gentle specifically to persuade the king to curb encomienda abuses. That makes his account strong evidence of how reformers framed the colonial debate, but weak evidence -- by itself -- for what Native societies were actually like before contact.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It assumes that because the author judged the conquest by timeless moral standards, his description of Native life must be accurate. Moral conviction tells us about his purpose, not about whether his portrait of Native society is balanced.
option_explanations.B: Right. His goal -- royal reform of colonial labor practices -- explains both why he wrote and what his account can and cannot establish. It documents the terms of the Spanish debate, but needs other evidence to describe Native societies themselves.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It makes violence the one and only cause of population collapse, ignoring introduced diseases and the disruption of forced labor. Even a firsthand witness can observe death without identifying every cause.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It takes one friar's description of Caribbean peoples and stretches it to all Native societies in the Americas, ignoring how different Native cultures were from one another.

items.fact_source: Las Casas held an encomienda in Hispaniola and renounced it c. 1515; his 1542 memorial to the crown helped prompt the New Laws of 1542. His portrait of Native peoples was shaped by his reform advocacy, in direct contrast to Sepulveda's 'natural slave' argument at the Valladolid debate of 1550-51.
